course.title: Uzbek, Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Modern Uzbek from absolute beginner through fluent, everyday command — real sentences, grammar, and conversational practice
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, built the same way as this app's Kazakh and Tajik courses.

a1-existence.title: There is/isn't: bor / yo'q
a1-existence.explanation: Bor and yo'q are standalone words that state whether something exists, with no verb "to be" involved at all: uyda non bor (there is bread at home), pulim yo'q (I don't have money, literally "my money doesn't-exist").
a1-existence.fact: Yo'q does double duty as both "there isn't/doesn't exist" and the everyday word for "no" in answer to a yes/no question -- the two uses come from exactly the same root idea of non-existence/negation.

dialogue.en: Is there tea at home?

dialogue.native: Yo'q, choy yo'q, faqat suv bor.
dialogue.en: No, there's no tea, only water.

a1-demonstratives.title: Demonstratives: bu / shu / u
a1-demonstratives.pattern: bu (this, near speaker) · shu (this, just mentioned) · u (that, far/absent)
a1-demonstratives.explanation: Bu points at something physically close to the speaker: bu kitob (this book, right here). U points at something distant or not present: u uy (that house, over there). Shu points back at something already mentioned in the conversation: shu masala (that matter [we were just discussing]).
a1-demonstratives.fact: Shu is the one English speakers most often reach for the wrong word for -- English "that" covers both u's distance and shu's "just-mentioned" sense, but Uzbek keeps them grammatically separate.

dialogue.en: Have you read this book?
Yes, I liked that book a lot.

a1-pronouns-tobe.title: Personal Pronouns & "To Be"
a1-pronouns-tobe.explanation: Uzbek has no separate verb 'to be' in the present tense — personal predicative endings attach directly to the noun or adjective, agreeing with the subject. Men talabaman (I am a student), sen talabasan (you are a student), u talaba (he/she is a student — no ending), biz talabamiz (we are students), siz talabasiz (you are a student, formal), ular talaba (they are students).
a1-pronouns-tobe.fact: Because 3rd person takes no ending at all, a bare sentence like "U shifokor" already means the complete "He/she is a doctor" — no word is missing, word order alone carries the meaning.

dialogue.en: Who are you? (formal)
I am a teacher. And you?
I am a student.

a1-possessive.title: Possessive Suffixes
a1-possessive.explanation: Uzbek marks possession with a suffix on the noun itself rather than a separate possessive pronoun: kitobim (my book), kitobing (your book), kitobi (his/her book), kitobimiz (our book), kitobingiz (your book, formal/plural), kitobi (their book — same as 3rd singular, context tells them apart).
a1-possessive.fact: The possessive suffix alone can carry a full meaning: onam by itself already means "my mother", with no separate word for "my" needed at all.

dialogue.en: Is this your book?
Yes, this is my book.

a1-plural.title: Plural: -lar
a1-plural.explanation: Uzbek marks the plural with a single invariant suffix, -lar, added to any noun regardless of its final sound: kitob → kitoblar (books), uy → uylar (houses), bola → bolalar (children).
a1-plural.fact: Unlike Kazakh or Turkish, standard Uzbek has largely lost vowel harmony, so -lar never changes shape (no -ler variant) — one suffix works for every noun in the language.

dialogue.en: How many rooms are there in the house?
There are three rooms in the house.

a1-questions.title: Yes/No Questions: -mi
a1-questions.explanation: To turn a statement into a yes/no question, Uzbek attaches the particle -mi directly to the word being questioned (not necessarily the verb): Bu kitobmi? (Is this a book?), Siz talabamisiz? (Are you a student?).
a1-questions.fact: Moving -mi to a different word in the same sentence shifts what's actually being asked: Siz talabamisiz? asks about being a student, while U sizmisiz? asks whether a specific person is you.

dialogue.en: Is this your house?
No, this is not my house.

a1-cases-1.title: Cases I: Dative & Locative (-ga, -da)
a1-cases-1.explanation: Uzbek marks direction with the dative suffix -ga (maktabga — to school) and location with the locative suffix -da (maktabda — at school). These attach directly to the noun with no separate preposition needed.
a1-cases-1.fact: The same suffix pair does double duty for time as well as place: bugun kechqurun-da works for "this evening" the same way uy-da works for "at home".

dialogue.en: Where are you going?
I'm going to the market.

a1-cases-2.title: Cases II: Accusative & Ablative (-ni, -dan)
a1-cases-2.explanation: The accusative suffix -ni marks a definite direct object: kitobni o'qiyman (I'm reading the book). The ablative suffix -dan marks origin or source: uydan chiqdim (I left the house / came out of the house).
a1-cases-2.fact: Leaving -ni off a direct object is grammatical too, but changes the meaning slightly toward something less specific — kitob o'qiyman ("I'm reading a book", general) versus kitobni o'qiyman ("I'm reading the book", a specific one).

dialogue.en: Where are you from?
I'm from Tashkent.

a1-present.title: Present-Future Tense: -(a)di
a1-present.explanation: Uzbek uses one tense form for both habitual present and future actions: boraman (I go / I will go), borasan, boradi, boramiz, borasiz, boradi(lar). Context makes clear whether it's a habit or a future plan.
a1-present.fact: The very same form men boraman can mean either "I go [there every day]" or "I will go [tomorrow]" — Uzbek doesn't force a speaker to choose between them the way English does.

dialogue.en: Will you go to the market tomorrow?
Yes, I'll go tomorrow.

a1-past.title: Simple Past: -di
a1-past.explanation: The simple past adds -di (or -ti after a voiceless consonant) directly to the verb stem: bordim (I went), bording, bordi, bordik, bordingiz, bordi(lar).
a1-past.fact: The 3rd person past form bordi looks identical whether the subject is singular or plural — u bordi (he/she went) and ular bordi (they went) are told apart only by the pronoun in front.

dialogue.en: Where did you go yesterday?
Yesterday I went to the market.

a1-negation.title: Negation: -ma- and emas
a1-negation.explanation: Verbs are negated by inserting -ma- right after the stem and before the tense ending: bormadim (I didn't go), boraman → bormayman (I don't/won't go). Nouns and adjectives, which have no verb to modify, use the separate word emas instead: talaba emasman (I am not a student).
a1-negation.fact: Because emas is a free-standing word rather than a suffix, it can be repeated on its own as a short "no, not that" answer — much like English "not" can stand alone in a quick correction.

dialogue.en: Are you a doctor?

dialogue.native: Yo'q, men shifokor emasman. Men o'qituvchiman.
dialogue.en: No, I am not a doctor. I am a teacher.

a2-frequency.title: Frequency Adverbs
a2-frequency.pattern: doim (always) · tez-tez (often) · ba'zan (sometimes) · kamdan-kam (rarely) · hech qachon (never)
a2-frequency.explanation: Frequency adverbs sit before the verb they describe: men doim erta turaman (I always wake up early), u kamdan-kam kinoga boradi (he/she rarely goes to the movies). Hech qachon requires a negative verb to agree with it: hech qachon yolg'on gapirmayman (I never lie).
a2-frequency.fact: Hech qachon literally combines hech ("any/none at all") with qachon ("when") -- "never" in Uzbek is grammatically "at no when", and it always needs that negative verb alongside it, since a bare positive verb with hech qachon would be ungrammatical, not just unusual.

dialogue.en: Do you often exercise?
Yes, almost every day.

a2-postpositions.title: Postpositions: bilan, uchun, kabi
a2-postpositions.explanation: Uzbek uses postpositions -- separate words placed AFTER the noun -- instead of English-style prepositions: do'stim bilan (with my friend), sen uchun (for you), sher kabi (like a lion).
a2-postpositions.fact: Bilan can also fuse onto the noun as a suffix in fast speech (do'stimla for do'stim bilan is common informally), but uchun and kabi always stay separate words -- not every postposition in Uzbek is equally free to cliticize.

dialogue.en: Who is this gift for?
It's for you, we chose it together with my friend.

a2-modal-can.title: Ability: -(a)olmoq ("can")
a2-modal-can.explanation: To express ability, Uzbek inserts ol (from olmoq, "to take/manage") right after the verb stem, before the tense ending: bora olaman (I can go), bora olmayman (I cannot go, negative adds -ma- before the tense ending too).
a2-modal-can.fact: The same ol also gives the language its word for "to get/receive" -- ability in Uzbek is literally framed as being able to "take" or "manage" an action, not a separate standalone modal verb the way English "can" is.

dialogue.en: Do you know how to swim?
Yes, I can swim.

a2-modal-kerak.title: Obligation: kerak ("must/should")
a2-modal-kerak.explanation: Obligation is expressed with the standalone word kerak after a possessive-marked infinitive: men borishim kerak (I must go, literally "my going is necessary"), sen borishing kerak (you must go).
a2-modal-kerak.fact: Because kerak is a free word rather than a suffix, it can also stand completely alone as a one-word answer meaning "[it's] necessary" -- much like English "must" can, but unlike most of Uzbek's other grammar markers, which are suffixes glued to the verb.

dialogue.en: Do I have to work today?
No, you can rest today.

a2-comparative.title: Comparative & Superlative
a2-comparative.explanation: The comparative adds -roq directly to an adjective: katta → kattaroq (bigger). The superlative simply places eng ("most") in front of the plain adjective: eng katta (the biggest) -- no separate ending needed for superlative.
a2-comparative.fact: Because -roq attaches to any adjective with no exceptions, Uzbek has no irregular comparatives at all -- there's no equivalent of English's good/better/best needing three separate words.

dialogue.en: Which house is bigger?
Our house is the biggest.

a2-imperative.title: Imperative
a2-imperative.explanation: An informal command is just the bare verb stem: bor! (go!). The formal/polite command adds -ing: boring! (please go!). Negative commands insert -ma right after the stem: borma! (don't go!), boring emas rather borma ni ng orqali - kelmang! (please don't come!, formal negative combines -ma and -ing: kel-ma-ng).
a2-imperative.fact: The formal negative imperative stacks BOTH markers onto one stem in a fixed order -- -ma before -ng, never the reverse (kelmang, never kelngma) -- one of the few places in Uzbek where suffix order is rigid rather than flexible.

dialogue.en: Please don't smoke here!
Sorry, of course I won't smoke.

a2-connectors.title: Connectors: chunki & shuning uchun
a2-connectors.explanation: Chunki ("because") introduces a reason after the main clause: Men uyda qoldim, chunki kasal edim (I stayed home because I was sick). Shuning uchun ("therefore/so") does the reverse, introducing a result after the reason: Kasal edim, shuning uchun uyda qoldim (I was sick, so I stayed home).
a2-connectors.fact: The two words let a speaker present the exact same two facts in either order -- reason-then-result or result-then-reason -- just by picking which connector goes in the middle, without changing either clause itself.

dialogue.en: Why didn't you come yesterday?

dialogue.native: Ishim ko'p edi, shuning uchun kela olmadim.
dialogue.en: I had a lot of work, so I couldn't come.

a2-present-continuous.title: Present Continuous: -(a)yap(ti)
a2-present-continuous.explanation: An action happening right now takes -yap (or -ayap after a consonant) plus a personal ending: yozayapman (I am writing), o'qiyapsan (you are reading), ishlayapti (he/she is working) -- distinct from the habitual/future -(a)di tense covered at A1.
a2-present-continuous.fact: Dropping the final -ti (yozayapman instead of the fuller yozayapti-man-like form) is so standard in everyday speech that the shorter form, not the technically fuller one, is what learners should treat as the default to imitate.

dialogue.en: What are you doing right now?
I'm reading a book.

a2-intention.title: Intention: -moqchi
a2-intention.explanation: To say what someone intends or plans to do, Uzbek adds -moqchi to the verb stem, then the usual predicative "to be" ending: bormoqchiman (I intend/plan to go), bormoqchisan (you plan to go), bormoqchi (he/she plans to go).
a2-intention.fact: -moqchi is built from -moq, the same ending that names a verb in its dictionary/infinitive form (bormoq = "to go") -- intention in Uzbek is grammatically framed as being oriented toward the bare infinitive itself, plus a state-of-being ending on top of it.

dialogue.en: What do you plan to do on the weekend?
I plan to go to the mountains.

b1-quantifiers.title: Quantifiers: har, hamma, ba'zi
b1-quantifiers.explanation: Har combines with a singular noun for "every": har kuni (every day), har bir odam (each and every person). Hamma stands alone for "everyone/everything": hamma biladi (everyone knows). Ba'zi precedes a noun for "some": ba'zi odamlar (some people).
b1-quantifiers.fact: Har always takes a SINGULAR noun even though its meaning is distributive/plural in effect (har bir odam, never har odamlar) -- much like English "every day" stays singular even while covering all days, Uzbek locks the noun to singular grammatically no matter how universal the meaning is.

dialogue.en: I wonder if everyone knows about this.
No, only some people know.

b1-purpose-sin-uchun.title: Purpose (3rd person): -sin uchun
b1-purpose-sin-uchun.explanation: To express purpose involving a third party ("so that he/she would..."), Uzbek combines the jussive -sin ("let him/her ~") with uchun: u tushunsin uchun tushuntirdim (I explained so that he/she would understand).
b1-purpose-sin-uchun.fact: This reuses -sin from its more basic "let him/her do it" command sense (kelsin! -- "let him/her come!") -- purpose-for-a-third-party in Uzbek is literally built as "so that [let-it-happen], I did X", folding a mild command into a purpose clause.

dialogue.en: Why did you write in such detail?
I wrote in detail so that everyone would understand.

b1-gan-participle.title: Experience/Result: -gan
b1-gan-participle.explanation: Uzbek has no separate present-perfect verb form the way English does ("have gone"); instead the participle -gan (voiced to -kan or -qan depending on the stem's last sound) plus a predicative ending covers both "has done X" and "did X, with present relevance": men bu filmni ko'rganman (I have seen this movie), u Parijga borgan (he/she has been to Paris).
b1-gan-participle.fact: The very same -gan form, without any predicative ending at all, also works as a plain adjective built from a verb: o'qigan kishi literally means "a person who has read/studied" -- i.e. an educated person -- one suffix covering both a full sentence and a single descriptive word.

dialogue.en: Have you been to this city?
Yes, I have been there twice.

b1-conditional.title: Conditional: -sa
b1-conditional.explanation: The conditional suffix -sa attaches directly to the verb stem, with the optional word agar ("if") added at the front for clarity: agar vaqtim bo'lsa, kelaman (if I have time, I'll come). The -sa clause always comes first, the result clause second.
b1-conditional.fact: Agar is genuinely optional -- vaqtim bo'lsa, kelaman means exactly the same thing without it -- because -sa alone already marks the clause as conditional; agar is there purely to flag the condition earlier for the listener, the way a comma-splice "if" softens a sentence in English but isn't grammatically required.

dialogue.native: Agar ertaga yomg'ir yog'sa, nima qilamiz?
dialogue.en: If it rains tomorrow, what will we do?
If it rains, we'll stay home.

b1-reported-speech.title: Reported Speech: deb
b1-reported-speech.explanation: Deb, a converb of demoq ("to say"), follows a quoted clause to mark it as reported speech or thought: Ertaga kelaman, deb aytdi (He/she said, "I will come tomorrow" / that he/she would come tomorrow). It can also report a belief or reason: kech qoldim, deb o'yladim (I thought I was late).
b1-reported-speech.fact: Deb is so productive it isn't limited to reporting speech at all -- it also marks the reason behind a naming or labeling, as in Toshkent, deb ataladi ("[it] is called Tashkent") -- the same tiny word bridges quotation, thought, and naming.

dialogue.en: What did he/she tell you?
He/she said that he/she would come tomorrow.

b1-concession.title: Concession: -sa ham / garchi
b1-concession.explanation: Adding ham ("also/even") after the conditional -sa turns "if" into "even if/although": yomg'ir yog'sa ham, boramiz (even if it rains, we'll go). Garchi ("although") can be added at the front for extra emphasis, but -sa ham alone already carries the full concessive meaning.
b1-concession.fact: This means Uzbek builds "although" out of the exact same conditional suffix used for plain "if" -- just by adding one small word, ham, after it -- rather than needing a completely different grammatical structure the way English switches from "if" to "although".

dialogue.en: Will you come even if you're tired?

dialogue.native: Ha, charchagan bo'lsam ham, albatta kelaman.
dialogue.en: Yes, even if I'm tired, I'll definitely come.

b1-passive.title: Passive Voice: -il / -in
b1-passive.explanation: The passive is formed by inserting -il (after most consonant-final stems) or -n (after vowel-final stems) between the verb stem and the tense ending: kitob o'qildi (the book was read), xat yozildi (the letter was written), eshik ochildi (the door was opened).
b1-passive.fact: Because the passive marker sits in the same slot as -a olmoq (ability) and -moqchi (intention), a single Uzbek verb stem can in principle carry several of these layered suffixes at once, each one shifting the meaning by a small, predictable step.

dialogue.en: When was this book written?
It was written in the last century.

b1-digan.title: General Participle: -digan
b1-digan.explanation: -digan turns a verb into a description of habitual or general action, working much like an English relative clause: o'qiydigan kitob ("a book that is read/for reading"), ishlaydigan joy ("a place where one works", i.e. a workplace).
b1-digan.fact: Unlike -gan (a specific, completed action), -digan describes something general or repeated -- kelgan kishi is "the person who came [that one time]", while keladigan kishi is "the person who [regularly/is going to] come" -- the same root, two different suffixes, two clearly different meanings.

dialogue.en: Are there any books to read here?

dialogue.native: Ha, javonda ko'p qiziqarli kitoblar bor.
dialogue.en: Yes, there are many interesting books on the shelf.

b1plus-opinion-cha.title: Opinion Marker: -cha
b1plus-opinion-cha.explanation: -cha attached to a possessive form frames a statement as someone's opinion or perspective: menimcha (in my opinion), sizningcha (in your opinion), uning fikricha (in his/her opinion, literally "according to his/her thought").
b1plus-opinion-cha.fact: Menimcha alone, with no further words, is a complete and extremely common way to open an opinion in conversation -- it functions the way "I think" does in English, but packs subject, verb-like meaning, and stance into a single suffixed word.

dialogue.en: In your opinion, is this decision correct?
In my opinion, yes, it's correct.

b1plus-result-connector.title: Result Connector: natijada
b1plus-result-connector.explanation: Natijada ("as a result") opens a new sentence to state the outcome of what was just described: u ko'p mashq qildi. Natijada, imtihonni a'lo topshirdi (He/she practiced a lot. As a result, he/she passed the exam with excellence.)
b1plus-result-connector.fact: Natijada is built from natija ("result/outcome") plus the locative -da ("in/at") -- it literally means "in the result", treating an outcome as a place the narrative has arrived at, the same way -da marks arriving "at" a physical location elsewhere in the grammar.

dialogue.en: Why is he/she so successful?

dialogue.native: Yillar davomida mehnat qildi. Natijada, hozirgi o'rniga yetdi.
dialogue.en: He/she worked for years. As a result, he/she reached his/her current position.

b1plus-causative.title: Causative: -tir / -dir / -t
b1plus-causative.explanation: The causative marks "making/letting someone do something": o'qimoq (to read/study) → o'qitmoq (to teach, literally "to make [someone] study"), yozmoq (to write) → yozdirmoq (to have [someone] write), kiymoq (to wear) → kiydirmoq (to dress someone).
b1plus-causative.fact: O'qitmoq ("to teach") is itself a causative built on o'qimoq ("to read/study") -- Uzbek doesn't have a separate root for "teach" at all, it's grammatically just "to cause to study".

dialogue.en: Who had you write this article?
My manager had me write it.

b1plus-until.title: Until: -guncha
b1plus-until.explanation: -guncha (with voiced variants -kuncha/-quncha) means "until [X happens]": u kelguncha kutaman (I'll wait until he/she comes), ish tugaguncha ishladik (we worked until the job was finished).
b1plus-until.fact: The same suffix also covers "the sooner ~, the better" comparisons in fixed phrases like ko'p gapirguncha, kam gapir ("rather than talking a lot, talk little") -- "until" and "rather than" turn out to share one grammatical shape in Uzbek.

dialogue.en: Until when will we wait?
We'll wait until he/she comes.

b1plus-before-after.title: Before/After a Verb: -madan oldin / -gandan keyin
b1plus-before-after.explanation: To sequence two actions, Uzbek attaches oldin ("before") to a negative-form-looking but neutral -madan and keyin ("after") to the -gan participle: ovqatlanmasdan oldin qo'l yuvaman (I wash my hands before eating), ovqatlanganimdan keyin dam olaman (after eating I rest).
b1plus-before-after.fact: -madan oldin looks like it contains the negative -ma-, but it isn't a negation here at all -- it's a fixed fossilized pattern meaning "before doing", one of several places where a suffix's shape and its usual meaning have quietly drifted apart.

dialogue.en: What do you do before sleeping?
I sleep after reading a book.

b1plus-optative.title: Wish: -sa edi
b1plus-optative.explanation: Adding edi (the past form of "to be") after the conditional -sa turns a condition into a wish about something not currently true: vaqtim bo'lsa edi... (if only I had time...), u shu yerda bo'lsa edi (if only he/she were here).
b1plus-optative.fact: This is the same -sa used for ordinary "if" clauses -- edi is the only thing that shifts the meaning from a real possibility to a wistful wish about something that isn't the case, much like English swaps "have" for "had" to mark the same shift.

dialogue.en: What do you wish for?
If only I had more time.

b1plus-permission.title: Permission/Possibility: -sa bo'ladi
b1plus-permission.explanation: -sa bo'ladi (literally "if ~, it becomes/works") asks or grants permission: bu yerda o'tirsa bo'ladimi? (may I sit here?), kirsa bo'ladi (you may enter). The negative bo'lmaydi denies it: bu yerda chekilsa bo'lmaydi (smoking is not allowed here).
b1plus-permission.fact: Because bo'lmoq means "to become/turn out", this construction literally asks "if [I do this], will it turn out okay?" -- permission in Uzbek is phrased as a check on the outcome, not a direct request for someone's approval the way English "may I" is.

dialogue.en: May I take a photo here?
Yes, you may.

b2-formal-nominalization.title: Formal Register Nominalizer: -moqlik
b2-formal-nominalization.explanation: Alongside the everyday -ish nominalizer, Uzbek has a more formal, bookish alternative built from -moq (the infinitive) plus -lik: o'qimoqlik ("the act of reading/studying") sits at a higher register than o'qish, and shows up more in academic or official writing than casual speech.
b2-formal-nominalization.fact: Because -moqlik is built directly on the infinitive/dictionary form rather than the bare stem, it reads as slightly more abstract and detached -- much the way English "the reading of" sounds more formal than the plain gerund "reading", even though both describe the identical action.

dialogue.en: How important is the preparing of this report?
Very important, the deadline is approaching.

b2-negative-conditional.title: Negative Conditional: -masa ("unless")
b2-negative-conditional.explanation: Adding the conditional -sa to an already-negated stem (-ma-) gives "unless": ishlamasang, pul topolmaysan (unless you work, you can't earn money -- literally "if you don't work"). It's the mirror image of the plain affirmative conditional covered earlier.
b2-negative-conditional.fact: Uzbek has no separate word for "unless" the way English does -- it's built compositionally from pieces already known (negative -ma, conditional -sa), which is why intermediate learners can produce it correctly the moment they've learned both suffixes separately, without memorizing anything new.

dialogue.native: Nima bo'lardi, agar u yordam bermasa?
dialogue.en: What would happen if he/she didn't help?

dialogue.native: U yordam bermasa, biz bu ishni bajara olmaymiz.
dialogue.en: Unless he/she helps, we can't complete this task.

b2-nominalization.title: Verbal Noun: -(i)sh
b2-nominalization.explanation: Adding -ish (or just -sh after a vowel) to a verb stem turns the action itself into an abstract noun that can be the subject or object of a sentence: kitob o'qish foydali (reading books is useful), sport bilan shug'ullanish sog'liqqa yaxshi (exercising is good for health).
b2-nominalization.fact: This same -ish is what dictionaries strip away to list a verb's bare stem -- o'qish ("reading") and o'qimoq ("to read", the citation form) share one root, just packaged for two different grammatical jobs: one as a noun, one as an infinitive label.

dialogue.en: In your opinion, is learning a foreign language difficult?
Regular practice makes it easier.

b2-purpose.title: Purpose: -ish uchun
b2-purpose.explanation: The verbal noun in -ish combines with uchun ("for/because of") to express purpose: pul topish uchun ishlayman (I work in order to earn money), imtihonga tayyorlanish uchun kutubxonaga bordim (I went to the library in order to prepare for the exam).
b2-purpose.fact: Uchun on its own is simply the word for "for" used with any noun (sen uchun, "for you") -- purpose clauses in Uzbek are built by feeding it a verbal noun instead of an ordinary one, not by inventing a separate "in order to" word the way English did.

dialogue.en: Why do you run every day?
I run in order to be healthy.

b2-wonder.title: Wondering: -mikan
b2-wonder.explanation: -mikan (from -mi, the question particle, plus ekan, "apparently/it seems") expresses genuine uncertainty or wondering, closer to "I wonder if..." than a direct question: u keladimikan? (I wonder if he/she will come?).
b2-wonder.fact: Because -mikan is built from the same -mi used for ordinary yes/no questions, it can be tacked onto almost any statement to soften it into a musing rather than a real question directed at a listener -- a way of thinking out loud grammatically.

dialogue.en: I wonder if the weather will be good tomorrow.
I don't know, we'll see.

b2-probability.title: Probability: -sa kerak
b2-probability.explanation: Kerak, already familiar from obligation ("must go"), also expresses probability when attached after a -sa form: u uyda bo'lsa kerak (he/she is probably at home) -- a guess based on evidence, not a requirement.
b2-probability.fact: The exact same word kerak covers both "you must" and "it must be [the case]" -- English needs two different senses of "must" for this too, but Uzbek marks the difference structurally: obligation uses a plain infinitive before kerak, probability uses the conditional -sa form.

dialogue.en: Why hasn't he/she come yet?
He/she is probably stuck on the way.

b2-relative-case.title: Participle + Case in Chained Clauses
b2-relative-case.explanation: A -gan/-digan participle clause can itself take a case ending once it modifies a noun that is then further marked: men o'qigan maktabning direktori (the principal of the school where I studied) -- the whole clause "the school where I studied" gets the genitive -ning before direktori attaches.
b2-relative-case.fact: This is how Uzbek builds what English needs a full relative clause plus a possessive for ("the principal OF the school WHERE I studied") out of a single chain of suffixes on ordinary nouns and participles, with no relative pronoun ("where", "which") anywhere in the sentence at all.

dialogue.en: Where is the company where you worked located?
It's located in the center of Tashkent.

b2plus-continuative.title: Continuative Aspect: -avermoq
b2plus-continuative.explanation: -avermoq (from -a + vermoq, "to give") marks an action continuing without stopping: u kutib turaverdi (he/she kept on waiting), gapiraverdi (he/she kept on talking). It can also soften a command into permission to continue: gapiraveringiz (please, go on talking).
b2plus-continuative.fact: Vermoq ("to give") turns up as a grammaticalized helper verb here with no sense of "giving" left at all -- it's been repurposed purely to mark that an action keeps going, one of several originally full verbs in Uzbek (bor-, ol-, tur-) that have been hollowed out into pure aspect markers.

dialogue.en: Is he/she still waiting?

dialogue.native: Ha, hech qayoqqa ketmay, kutib turaverdi.
dialogue.en: Yes, without going anywhere, he/she kept on waiting.

b2plus-converb-reduplication.title: Converb Reduplication for Vividness
b2plus-converb-reduplication.explanation: Repeating a converb in -(i)b back-to-back paints a vivid, drawn-out picture of an action happening repeatedly or continuously alongside the main clause: yig'lab-yig'lab gapirdi (he/she spoke while crying and crying / spoke through repeated tears), kulib-kulib hikoya qildi (he/she told the story laughing and laughing).
b2plus-converb-reduplication.fact: This reduplication is a purely stylistic intensifier -- yig'lab gapirdi (single converb) and yig'lab-yig'lab gapirdi both mean "spoke while crying", but only the doubled form conveys that the crying was repeated, drawn-out, or emotionally heightened, the way English might reach for "crying and crying" instead of just "crying".

dialogue.en: How did he/she tell the story?
Crying and crying, he/she barely managed to speak.

b2plus-past-unreal.title: Past Unreal Conditional: -gan bo'lsa edi / -gan bo'lardi
b2plus-past-unreal.explanation: To talk about a past that didn't happen, Uzbek combines the -gan participle with bo'lsa edi in the "if" clause and bo'lardi (the conditional of bo'lmoq) in the result: agar bilganimda edi, kelmagan bo'lardim (if I had known, I wouldn't have come).
b2plus-past-unreal.fact: Every piece of this construction is independently familiar from earlier levels (-gan, edi, -sa, bo'lmoq) -- B2+ fluency here is less about learning new suffixes and more about correctly stacking four already-known ones in the right order.

dialogue.native: Agar u yerda bo'lganingizda, nima qilardingiz?
dialogue.en: If you had been there, what would you have done?
I would have helped immediately.

b2plus-emphatic-ku.title: Emphatic Particle: -ku
b2plus-emphatic-ku.explanation: -ku attaches to the end of a clause to add assertive emphasis, roughly "you know" or "after all": men aytdim-ku! (I did tell you!/I told you, didn't I!). It signals the speaker feels the point should already be obvious or agreed on.
b2plus-emphatic-ku.fact: -ku carries a faintly argumentative or exasperated tone -- it's the grammatical equivalent of raising your eyebrows while saying something, and overusing it in formal writing reads as oddly confrontational.

dialogue.en: Why didn't you tell me?
I did tell you, you just didn't listen!

b2plus-axir.title: Discourse Marker: axir
b2plus-axir.explanation: Axir ("after all/but") opens a clause that reminds the listener of something relevant they seem to have overlooked: axir men senga aytgandim (after all, I did tell you), axir u hali yosh (but he/she is still young, after all).
b2plus-axir.fact: Axir and -ku often appear in the very same sentence for double emphasis (axir aytdim-ku!, "but I DID tell you, after all!") -- Uzbek stacks its emphatic markers rather than treating them as mutually exclusive alternatives.

dialogue.en: Why don't you believe this?
But this sounds very strange, after all.

b2plus-converb-chain.title: Converb Chains: -ib
b2plus-converb-chain.explanation: The converb -ib links a sequence of actions by the same subject into one flowing sentence, with only the LAST verb carrying full tense marking: turib, kiyinib, ishga bordim (I got up, got dressed, and went to work) -- literally "getting up, getting dressed, I-went to work".
b2plus-converb-chain.fact: Only the final verb in the chain shows person and tense at all -- turib and kiyinib are grammatically bare converbs, not separate finite verbs -- so a very long chain of actions can rest on a single tensed verb at the very end of the sentence.

dialogue.en: What did you do in the evening?
I ate, read a book, and went to sleep.

b2plus-double-negative.title: Emphatic Double Negative: -may qolmaydi
b2plus-double-negative.pattern: [verb stem] + -may qolmaydi (won't fail to ~ / is bound to ~)
b2plus-double-negative.explanation: Combining the negative converb -may with qolmaydi ("won't remain/stay") produces a strong positive claim through double negation: u kelmay qolmaydi (he/she won't fail to come = he/she is bound to come).
b2plus-double-negative.fact: The two negatives (-may and qol-may-di's own negative) don't cancel out to plain neutral certainty -- they combine into something stronger and more emphatic than the simple affirmative u albatta keladi would sound, similar to how English "won't NOT come" reads as more forceful than a flat "will come".

dialogue.en: I wonder if he/she will come to the meeting.
Of course he'll/she'll come, he/she is bound to.

c1-speaker-inference.title: Speaker's Own Inference: shekilli
c1-speaker-inference.pattern: [clause] + shekilli (it seems/apparently, based on what I observe)
c1-speaker-inference.explanation: Shekilli hedges a claim as the SPEAKER's own inference from visible evidence, distinct from ekan (a fresh discovery), emish (distanced hearsay), and -mikan (wondering aloud): u charchagan shekilli (he/she seems tired [judging by how he/she looks]).
c1-speaker-inference.fact: Uzbek grammatically distinguishes at least four flavors of "apparently" that English collapses into one word -- shekilli (my own visual/contextual inference), ekan (a fact I just discovered), emish (something I heard secondhand, held at a distance), and -mikan (my own open-ended wondering) -- and mixing them up is one of the clearest tells of a non-native speaker at this level.

dialogue.en: Why is he/she so quiet?
He/she seems tired, worked all day.

c1-on-the-verge.title: On the Verge Of: -gudek
c1-on-the-verge.pattern: [verb stem] + -gudek + bo'lmoq (to be on the verge of ~ing / to such an extent that ~)
c1-on-the-verge.explanation: -gudek combined with bo'lmoq expresses being right on the edge of an action or state: yig'lagudek bo'ldi (he/she was on the verge of crying). It can also intensify a description to an extreme degree: kulgudek gap emas (it's not a laughing matter, literally "not talk to the extent of laughing").
c1-on-the-verge.fact: -gudek shares its -dek ending with the plain simile suffix (sher dek, "like a lion") and with -gandek ("as if") -- all three compare something to a reference point, but -gudek's reference point is a threshold not yet crossed, making it the only one of the three pointing at something imminent rather than already true or merely apparent.

dialogue.native: U bu xabarni eshitib nima qildi?
dialogue.en: What did he/she do upon hearing this news?

dialogue.native: Yig'lagudek bo'ldi, ammo o'zini tutib qoldi.
dialogue.en: He/she was on the verge of crying, but held himself/herself together.

c1-as-if.title: As If: -gandek
c1-as-if.explanation: Adding dek ("like/as") to the -gan participle creates "as if": u hammasini bilgandek gapirdi (he/she spoke as if he/she knew everything). It expresses a comparison to an event presented as unreal or merely apparent.
c1-as-if.fact: Dek is the same comparative word used in plain similes (sher dek kuchli, "strong as a lion") -- "as if" in Uzbek is grammatically just a simile whose point of comparison happens to be an entire completed action instead of a noun.

dialogue.en: Why is he/she so calm?
He/she is acting as if nothing happened.

c1-factual-concession.title: Factual Concession: -gani bilan
c1-factual-concession.pattern: [verb stem] + -gan + i + bilan (despite the fact that ~)
c1-factual-concession.explanation: -gani bilan (the -gan participle, possessive -i, plus bilan, "with") concedes a FACT already known to be true, unlike the more hypothetical -sa ham: boy bo'lgani bilan, baxtli emas (despite being rich, he/she isn't happy) presupposes that he/she really is rich.
c1-factual-concession.fact: Because -gani bilan presupposes the conceded fact is real, while -sa ham works for both real and merely hypothetical concessions, native speakers reach for -gani bilan specifically when they want to flag "yes, that part is definitely true, but..." -- a nuance that's easy to blur at lower levels.

dialogue.native: U juda boy-ku, nega xursand emas?
dialogue.en: He/she is very rich, so why isn't he/she happy?
Despite being rich, he/she isn't happy.

c1-embedded-subject.title: Embedded Clause as Subject: -(i)shi
c1-embedded-subject.explanation: A possessive-marked verbal noun lets a whole clause act as the grammatical subject of another sentence: uning kelishi meni xursand qildi ("his/her coming made me happy", i.e. "the fact that he/she came made me happy") -- uning is genitive "his/her", kelishi is "coming" with a matching 3rd-person possessive ending.
c1-embedded-subject.fact: The possessive ending on the verbal noun must agree with whoever performs the embedded action, not with the main sentence's subject -- uning kelishi ("his/her coming") keeps that -i ending no matter who is made happy by it, exactly the way mening kitobim ("my book") agrees with the owner, not the sentence's grammatical subject.

dialogue.en: Why are you so happy?

dialogue.native: Uning kelishi meni juda xursand qildi.
dialogue.en: His/her coming made me very happy.

c1-hearsay.title: Hearsay/Doubt: emish
c1-hearsay.explanation: Emish marks reported information the speaker isn't personally vouching for, often with a hint of skepticism: u mashhur olim emish (he/she is allegedly a famous scientist [so I've heard, but I'm not sure]).
c1-hearsay.fact: Emish carries a distancing, sometimes slightly doubtful tone that -deb aytdi (plain reported speech, covered at B1) doesn't -- choosing emish over a neutral report is itself a small signal to the listener that the speaker isn't fully endorsing the claim.

dialogue.en: They say he/she has bought a new car.
Really? He's/she's allegedly a very rich person, apparently.

c2-thwarted-intention.title: Thwarted Past Intention: -moqchi bo'lgan edi
c2-thwarted-intention.pattern: [verb stem] + -moqchi + bo'lgan edi, lekin/ammo [what prevented it]
c2-thwarted-intention.explanation: Layering the past perfect edi onto -moqchi bo'lmoq (already "to intend to") pushes the intention itself into the past and implies it didn't pan out: u kelmoqchi bo'lgan edi, lekin kelolmadi (he/she had intended to come, but couldn't). Without a following lekin-clause, the thwarted reading is only implied, not certain.
c2-thwarted-intention.fact: Every piece here (-moqchi, bo'lmoq, -gan, edi) was already familiar from earlier levels -- true C2 command of this construction is entirely about recognizing that stacking them onto ONE VERB shifts "I intend" all the way to "I had intended, but didn't follow through", with no new suffix to learn at all.

dialogue.en: Didn't he/she come to the celebration?

dialogue.native: Kelmoqchi bo'lgan edi, lekin kasal bo'lib qoldi.
dialogue.en: He/she had intended to come, but fell ill.

c2-rhetorical-question.title: Rhetorical Assertion: -madimmi? / -mas edimi?
c2-rhetorical-question.pattern: [negative statement] + -mi? (a question that asserts the opposite)
c2-rhetorical-question.explanation: A negative statement turned into a question asserts its positive opposite with rhetorical force: men aytmadimmi? (didn't I say so? = I certainly did say so), bu to'g'ri emasmidi? (wasn't this correct? = this was clearly correct). No answer is actually expected.
c2-rhetorical-question.fact: This is the same -mi question particle used for genuine yes/no questions everywhere else in the language -- what makes it rhetorical is purely that the speaker already knows and expects the listener to agree with the answer, a pragmatic effect layered on top of ordinary question grammar rather than a separate rhetorical suffix.

dialogue.en: This plan ended in failure.
Didn't I say this would happen?

c2-immediately-after.title: Immediately After: -gach
c2-immediately-after.explanation: -gach marks one action as happening immediately upon the completion of another, tighter in sequence than the more neutral -gandan keyin: u kelgach, boshladik (as soon as he/she arrived, we started) implies almost no gap between the two events.
c2-immediately-after.fact: -gach is a converb that never takes a personal ending at all, unlike -gan (which does when used predicatively) -- it exists purely to glue one clause tightly to the next, with the sentence's real tense and person carried entirely by the final verb.

dialogue.en: As soon as you received the news, what did you do?
As soon as I received it, I called immediately.

c2-esa.title: Contrastive Topic: esa
c2-esa.explanation: Esa marks a shift in topic with an implied contrast, close to "as for X.../whereas": men choy ichaman, u esa qahva ichadi (I drink tea, whereas he/she drinks coffee). It highlights the new topic against what was just said, without needing a separate word for "but".
c2-esa.fact: Esa can also stand at the very start of a clause with no preceding contrast at all, simply to mark "now, about this..." when shifting attention to a new subject -- its contrastive reading comes from context, not from any built-in meaning of opposition.

dialogue.en: Do you like sports?

dialogue.native: Men futbolni yoqtiraman, akam esa shaxmatni afzal ko'radi.
dialogue.en: I like football, whereas my older brother prefers chess.

c2-evidential-ekan.title: Mirative/Evidential: ekan
c2-evidential-ekan.explanation: Ekan marks information the speaker has just realized or learned indirectly, without the skepticism emish carries: u juda mehnatkash ekan (it turns out he/she is very hard-working) reports a fresh realization, treated as reliable, not doubted hearsay.
c2-evidential-ekan.fact: Ekan and emish both mark information not witnessed firsthand, but they split "apparently" into two flavors English doesn't distinguish grammatically: ekan for a neutral, credible discovery, emish for something the speaker is holding at arm's length -- choosing the wrong one subtly misrepresents how much the speaker actually believes it.

dialogue.en: What kind of person does he/she turn out to be?
He/she turns out to be very kind.

c2-poetic-yu.title: Elevated Coordination: -u / -yu
c2-poetic-yu.explanation: The enclitic -u (after a consonant) or -yu (after a vowel) links a pair into one vivid, often emotionally heightened image: kechayu kunduz (night and day, ceaselessly), yig'lay-yig'lay gapirdi is plain repetition, but kuni-yu tuni ishladi (he/she worked day and night) uses -u/-yu to fuse the pair into a single continuous stretch of time.
c2-poetic-yu.fact: This coordination is reserved for elevated or literary register -- swapping it for the plain conjunction va (kun va tun, "day and va night") is grammatically fine but strips out the sense of relentless, unbroken continuity that -u/-yu specifically signals.

dialogue.native: U bu loyiha ustida qanday ishladi?
dialogue.en: How did he/she work on this project?
He/she worked tirelessly, night and day.

c2-formal-passive-causative.title: Formal Register: Stacked Passive-Causative
c2-formal-passive-causative.explanation: Bureaucratic and legal Uzbek often stacks the causative and passive on one stem for an impersonal, formal tone: ko'rib chiqilishi so'raladi ("it is requested that [it] be reviewed") distances the sentence from any named actor entirely -- nobody is said to be doing or requesting anything, only that reviewing-of-it is being requested.
c2-formal-passive-causative.fact: This stacked, actor-erasing structure is essentially never used in casual speech -- reaching for it (rather than a plain active sentence with a named subject) is itself a register marker, signaling "this is an official document" the same way passive constructions do in formal English.

dialogue.en: When will the application be reviewed?
It is requested that it be reviewed within the established period.

paragraphs.native: Donishmandlik yillar bilan emas, balki tajriba bilan o'lchanadi, deyishadi.

paragraphs.en: For this reason, we must value our own path, not someone else's.
